The Raven Mocker reaches through the walls — through wood, through stone, through the fabric of the living world — and takes the remaining years of the dying person's life. It steals them like a thief stealing corn, drawing them out in pale, luminous threads that the creature absorbs into its own body.

The Raven Mockers eat the hearts of the dead. After the last breath has been drawn and the spirit has departed, the creatures tear open the chest and consume the heart, which they believe holds the essence of a person's remaining years. By eating the heart, the Raven Mocker adds those years to its own寿命, living far beyond the span of any mortal.

The only defense against a Raven Mocker is a medicine man who knows the proper rituals — songs of protection, herbs that create a barrier of sacred smoke, prayers that call upon the Thunder Beings for strength. Some medicine men could see the Raven Mockers even in their human form, recognizing them by their sleepless eyes and the faint smell of death that clung to their clothing. These medicine men would warn families when a Raven Mocker was near, and they would stand vigil at the bedsides of the dying, singing the songs that kept the creatures at bay.

But not all medicine men could see them, and not all families could afford the protection. The Raven Mockers were most active in times of plague and hardship, when death was common and the medicine men were spread thin. In those dark times, the creatures flew in packs — three, five, seven at a time — their wings beating the night sky into a frenzy, their cries mixing with the wind until the whole mountain seemed to howl.

The Cherokee speak of the Raven Mockers with a reverence that borders on terror. They are not simply monsters — they are a reminder that death is not always a clean break, that there are forces that feed on suffering, that the boundary between life and death is not a wall but a doorway, and that doorway has guardians who are not kind.

To this day, when someone in a Cherokee community falls gravely ill, the elders gather. They do not speak of Raven Mockers directly — that would give them power — but they light the sacred fire, burn the cleansing herbs, and sing the old songs. They stand watch through the long nights, and they do not leave until the sick person either recovers or has passed beyond the reach of the Kâ'lanû Ahkyeli'skï.

The Raven Mockers still fly. They fly on the darkest nights, when the moon is new and the clouds are thick, and their wings make no sound that human ears can hear. But the medicine men hear them. They always hear them.

title: The Rabbit Trickster (Chickasaw)
summary: Chukfi (or Chokfi), the Rabbit, is the trickster figure in Chickasaw folklore. Rabbit is clever, mischievous, and always getting into trouble, but he also uses his wits to benefit the people. In one story, Rabbit outwits the wolves by pretending to be dead and then escaping when they are not looking. In another, he tricks the larger animals into letting him share their food. Rabbit's adventures explain many natural phenomena, such as why Rabbit has a short tail, why the possum's tail is bare, and why the deer has antlers. Though Rabbit is often selfish and deceitful, his cleverness is admired, and his stories teach important lessons about the consequences of pride, greed, and dishonesty. Listeners are encouraged to laugh at Rabbit's antics while learning from his mistakes.
full_text:
Chukfi, the Rabbit, is the trickster figure in Chickasaw folklore — a creature of boundless energy, limitless cunning, and absolutely no shame. He is clever, mischievous, and always getting into trouble, but he also uses his wits to benefit the people — though usually by accident.

In one story, Rabbit outwits the wolves by pretending to be dead. He lies in the middle of the trail, his body limp, his eyes closed, his tongue hanging out. The wolves find him and, believing him dead, drag him to their den, planning to eat him later. But while the wolves are away hunting, Rabbit wakes up, eats their food, and escapes through a hole in the back of the den. When the wolves return, they find their food gone and Rabbit gone with it.

In another story, Rabbit tricks the larger animals into letting him share their food. He tells the Deer that the Bear has offered to share his honey, and tells the Bear that the Deer has offered to share his corn, and tells both of them that the Turkey has offered to share his berries. When they all arrive at the same clearing, carrying their gifts, they find Rabbit already there, sitting in the center, waiting for the feast.

Rabbit's adventures explain many natural phenomena. Why Rabbit has a short tail? Because he lost a bet with the Squirrel and had to give up most of his tail. Why the Possum's tail is bare? Because Rabbit tricked the Possum into putting his tail in a tree stump, and when the Possum pulled it out, the fur stayed behind. Why the Deer has antlers? Because Rabbit convinced the Deer that antlers would make him look more regal, and the Deer believed him.

Though Rabbit is often selfish and deceitful, his cleverness is admired. The Chickasaw do not hate Rabbit for his tricks; they laugh at him, because they see themselves in him — the desire to get something for nothing, the willingness to bend the truth, the ability to turn a bad situation into a good one through sheer audacity.

His stories teach important lessons about the consequences of pride, greed, and dishonesty. Rabbit always pays for his tricks, eventually — a sore foot, a lost tail, a meal that turns out to be a trap. Listeners are encouraged to laugh at Rabbit's antics while learning from his mistakes.

title: Raven Steals the Sun, Moon, and Stars (Haida)
summary: In the time before light, Raven (Nang Kilslas) was tired of living in darkness. He discovered an old chief who kept all the light of the universe hidden in a nested set of five boxes. Raven transformed himself into a hemlock needle and dropped into the river where the chief's daughter came to drink. She swallowed the needle and became pregnant, giving birth to Raven-child. The old chief adored his grandchild. Raven cried incessantly until the chief allowed him to open the boxes one by one. First the stars escaped, then the moon, then the northern lights. Finally Raven grabbed the sun in his beak and flew through the smoke hole, releasing light into the world forever. This core Haida myth explains the origin of all celestial light and establishes Raven as both a trickster and culture hero who brought essential gifts to humanity despite his selfish motives.
source: Haida oral tradition; John Reed Swanton, Haida Texts and Myths; The Earth Stories Collection
full_text:
In the time before light, when the world was draped in a darkness so complete that the people could not tell friend from foe, land from water, or earth from sky, Raven — Nang Kilslas — was tired of living in darkness. He was tired of stumbling through the forest, tired of tripping over roots he could not see, tired of the way the darkness pressed against his eyes like a hand against a face.

Raven discovered an old chief who kept all the light of the universe hidden in a nested set of five boxes. The boxes were made of cedar, each one smaller than the last, fitted inside each other with the precision of a master carver. Inside the innermost box was the sun. Inside the next was the moon. Inside the third were the stars. The fourth held the northern lights, and the fifth held the dawn. The old chief guarded these treasures with a vigilance born of the knowledge that light was the most valuable thing in the world.

Raven transformed himself into a hemlock needle — small, sharp, and ordinary — and dropped into the river where the chief's daughter came to drink. She was young and beautiful, and when she saw the needle floating on the water, she bent to drink. She swallowed the needle without thinking, and it lodged inside her, and she became pregnant.

She gave birth to Raven-child. The old chief adored his grandchild. The child was beautiful — dark-eyed, bright-skinned, with a laugh that filled the house like sunlight. But the child cried incessantly. He cried at dawn, he cried at dusk, he cried through the night until the chief could not sleep and the house shook with the force of the child's grief.

The chief tried everything. He gave the child food, water, toys, songs. Nothing worked. The child cried and cried, until at last the chief, desperate for peace, allowed him to open the boxes one by one.

First the stars escaped, shooting from the box like sparks from a fire, scattering across the sky. Then the moon rose, pale and round, casting a soft glow over the world. Then the northern lights danced, their green and purple curtains rippling across the sky. Finally Raven grabbed the sun in his beak — his true beak, for he had shed his human form — and flew through the smoke hole of the chief's house, releasing light into the world forever.

The sun blazed across the sky, and the world was transformed. The trees were green, the water was blue, the mountains were gray and massive and beautiful. The people looked up and wept with joy, for they had never seen the world before.

This core Haida myth explains the origin of all celestial light and establishes Raven as both a trickster and culture hero who brought essential gifts to humanity despite his selfish motives. Raven did not steal the light for the people — he stole it for himself, because he was tired of the dark. But the result was the same: the world was lit, and humanity benefited from Raven's selfishness.

title: Raven and the Moon Woman (Haida)
summary: Raven became the son of Moon Woman and cried incessantly, saying 'Boo-hoo, moon!' His mother, exhausted by his noise, stopped up all the holes in the house and untied the strings of a box containing the moon, letting Raven play with it. When she left, Raven turned into a raven and flew about the house with the moon in his beak. He then cried for the smoke hole to be opened, and when his mother obliged, he flew through it with the moon under his wing. He perched on a house top and called like a raven. Raven flew to the Nass River where fishermen were taking olachen in total darkness. He bargained with them, offering light in exchange for their spruce needles. When they mocked him, he let them see a sliver of the moon, and they gave him many olachen. He then flew to a high mountain, broke the moon in half, threw one half into the sky for the night and the other for the day, and scattered fragments as stars.
source: Haida oral tradition; Wikisource Myths and Legends of British North America
full_text:
Raven became the son of Moon Woman. He cried incessantly, a wail that filled the house and shook the walls: 'Boo-hoo, moon! Boo-hoo, moon!' His mother, exhausted by his noise, tried everything to quiet him. She sang to him, she fed him, she rocked him in her arms. Nothing worked. The child cried and cried, his voice high and piercing, until the walls of the house trembled.

At last, Moon Woman stopped up all the holes in the house — the door, the windows, the gaps between the planks — and untied the strings of a box containing the moon. She let Raven play with it, hoping the sight of the glowing sphere would calm him.

Raven stopped crying. He held the moon in his hands, turning it this way and that, watching the light play across his fingers. He seemed content. But when his mother left the house, Raven changed. He turned into a raven — his true form, black-feathered and sharp-eyed — and flew about the house with the moon in his beak.

He cried for the smoke hole to be opened, and when his mother obliged, he flew through it with the moon under his wing. He perched on a house top and called like a raven, his voice echoing across the village.

Raven flew to the Nass River where fishermen were taking olachen in total darkness. The olachen — candlefish, fat and bright — were the wealth of the river people, and they caught them by the light of torches made from split alder. But the darkness was thick, and the torches gave little light, and the fishermen struggled.

Raven bargained with them, offering light in exchange for their spruce needles — the needles that the fishermen used to weave their nets. When they mocked him, he let them see a sliver of the moon — just enough to light the river, just enough to show the fish. The fishermen were astonished, and they gave him many olachen.

He then flew to a high mountain, broke the moon in half, threw one half into the sky for the night and the other for the day, and scattered fragments as stars. The night sky blazed with light, and the fishermen could see their nets, their boats, and the faces of their companions.

This story explains the origin of the moon and the stars, and it establishes Raven as a being who brings gifts through trickery — not out of generosity, but out of a combination of selfishness, cleverness, and a strange, reluctant compassion.

title: Raven Steals the Light (Tlingit - Yeil)
summary: In the Tlingit version of this foundational myth, Yeil (Raven) was born as the son of Kit-ka'ositiyi-qâ and was instructed and trained in every way to make a world. At that time there was no light in the world, but Raven knew that far up the Nass River was a large house where a chief kept light just for himself. Raven turned himself into a pine needle and dropped into the drinking cup of the chief's daughter. She swallowed it and gave birth to Raven as a human baby. The grandfather loved the child and eventually gave him the bundles containing the stars. Raven scattered them across the sky. He cried for the moon and pushed it through the smoke hole. Finally he cried for the box of daylight, turned into his true raven form, and flew out with the daylight under his wing. The Tlingit version emphasizes Raven's dual nature as creator and trickster, and explains not only the origin of light but also the creation of human beings from leaves after the great flood.
source: John R. Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts (1909); Tlingit oral tradition
full_text:
In the Tlingit version of this foundational myth, Yeil — Raven — was born as the son of Kit-ka'ositiyi-qan, a being of immense power who instructed and trained his son in every way to make a world. At that time there was no light in the world, but Raven knew that far up the Nass River was a large house where a chief kept light just for himself.

Raven turned himself into a pine needle — small, green, ordinary — and dropped into the drinking cup of the chief's daughter. She swallowed it without thinking, and she became pregnant, and she gave birth to Raven as a human baby.

The grandfather loved the child. The baby was beautiful — dark-eyed, bright-skinned, with a laugh that echoed through the house like the sound of water over stones. But the baby cried. He cried incessantly, his voice rising and falling with a rhythm that was almost musical but relentlessly demanding. The grandfather tried everything to quiet him — food, water, songs, toys. Nothing worked.

At last, the grandfather offered the child the bundles containing the stars. Raven stopped crying. He opened the bundle and scattered the stars across the sky, and the world was lit — not brightly, but enough. The stars burned in their fixed positions, each one a point of light in the vast darkness.

Raven cried for the moon. The grandfather offered the moon, and Raven pushed it through the smoke hole of the house. It rose into the sky, pale and round, casting a soft glow over the world.

Finally, Raven cried for the box of daylight. The grandfather, exhausted by the child's demands, gave him the box. Raven opened it, turned into his true raven form — black-feathered, sharp-eyed, enormous — and flew out of the house with the daylight under his wing. He soared across the sky, and the world blazed with light.

The Tlingit version emphasizes Raven's dual nature as creator and trickster, and explains not only the origin of light but also the creation of human beings from leaves after the great flood. Raven brought light to the world, but he did not do it for the people — he did it for himself. The fact that humanity benefited was, as with most of Raven's deeds, an accidental kindness.

title: Raven and the Fog Woman (Tlingit)
summary: Raven wanted to marry and went to the chief called Fog-Over-The-Salmon, who had a young daughter. The chief agreed but made Raven promise to treat her with respect. They married and lived contentedly through summer and fall, but winter brought famine. Raven's wife began making a basket, and despite Raven's testy comments, she completed it. The next morning she washed her hands in the basket and salmon appeared, the first salmon ever created. Every day she did this and their house was soon full of drying salmon. But Raven forgot his good fortune and quarreled with his wife daily. In a rage, he hit her with a piece of dried salmon. She fled toward the water, and when Raven tried to catch her, his hands passed through her body as if through mist. All the salmon followed her into the sea. She disappeared into the fog, for she was Fog Woman herself. Raven went to his father-in-law to beg for her return, but Chief Fog-Over-The-Salmon refused, saying Raven had broken his promise.
source: John R. Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts (1909); Tlingit oral tradition adapted by University of Alaska Fairbanks
full_text:
Raven wanted to marry and went to the chief called Fog-Over-The-Salmon, who had a young daughter. The chief was a powerful being — his house stood at the edge of the water, and the fog that rose from the river each morning was his breath. He agreed to the marriage but made Raven promise to treat his daughter with respect.

They married and lived contentedly through summer and fall. Raven's wife was quiet and industrious, and she kept the house in order while Raven fished and hunted. But winter brought famine. The salmon were gone, the berries were buried under snow, and the people grew hungry.

Raven's wife began making a basket. It was a large basket, woven from cedar bark, and she worked on it slowly, patiently, despite Raven's testy comments about the time she spent on it. 'Why do you waste your time on that basket?' he asked. 'We have no food, no firewood, no warmth, and you sit here weaving.' But the woman said nothing, and she continued to work.

The next morning she washed her hands in the basket. She dipped her hands into the water she had poured into it, and when she lifted them out, a salmon lay in the basket — the first salmon ever created. Every day she did this, and their house was soon full of drying salmon. The smell of smoking fish filled the air, and Raven's hunger was satisfied.

But Raven forgot his good fortune. He quarreled with his wife daily, complaining about the food, about the house, about the cold. In a rage, he hit her with a piece of dried salmon. The blow was hard enough to leave a mark, and it broke something between them — a bond that could not be repaired.

She fled toward the water. When Raven tried to catch her, his hands passed through her body as if through mist. She was becoming fog, becoming water, becoming the river itself. All the salmon followed her into the sea. She disappeared into the fog, for she was Fog Woman herself.

Raven went to his father-in-law to beg for her return, but Chief Fog-Over-The-Salmon refused. 'You broke your promise,' he said. 'You did not treat her with respect. She will not come back.' And she never did.

title: Raven Pulls the Salmon (Tlingit)
summary: After Raven brought light to the world and created rivers and lakes, there were still no salmon in the coastal waters. The salmon, herrings, and ooligans were kept in a magical house in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, where they spawned without ever coming to shore. Only rich chiefs could paddle out to catch them, leaving the poor hungry. Raven heard of Xanaax.atwaayaa, a mythical being who possessed an octopus-tentacle staff with supernatural powers. Raven tricked the being into trading the staff by demonstrating a magical bow and arrow (actually a magpie) that seemed to kill a mountain goat from impossible distances. With the staff, Raven went to the entrance of the Alsek River and latched it to the salmon house. He struggled mightily, and his nephew Crow urged him to sing a song about Xanaax.atwaayaa. When Raven sang, he easily pulled all the salmon into the bays and rivers. The tracks of Raven's struggle can still be seen at the Alsek River entrance.
source: Tlingit legend as told by Henry Davis, Sheldon Jackson College; University of Alaska Fairbanks curriculum
full_text:
After Raven brought light to the world and created rivers and lakes, there were still no salmon in the coastal waters. The salmon, herrings, and ooligans were kept in a magical house in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, where they spawned without ever coming to shore. Only rich chiefs could paddle out to catch them, leaving the poor hungry.

Raven heard of Xanaax.atwaayaa, a mythical being who possessed an octopus-tentacle staff with supernatural powers. The staff was long and flexible, covered in suckers that gripped whatever they touched, and it could pull anything toward its holder — fish, canoes, even the tide itself.

Raven tricked the being into trading the staff by demonstrating a magical bow and arrow that seemed to kill a mountain goat from impossible distances. The bow was actually a magpie, and the arrow was actually the magpie's beak — Raven had trained the bird to fly toward the goat and peck it, and the goat had fallen, and Xanaax.atwaayaa had believed the bow was responsible.

With the staff, Raven went to the entrance of the Alsek River and latched it to the salmon house. He struggled mightily — the staff was heavy, the current was strong, and the salmon house was anchored to the bottom of the ocean. His nephew Crow urged him to sing a song about Xanaax.atwaayaa.

When Raven sang, he easily pulled all the salmon into the bays and rivers. The salmon leaped from the water, their silver bodies flashing in the sun, their tails beating the surface into foam. They swam up the rivers, spawning in the gravel beds, and from them came the abundance that sustained the coastal peoples.

The tracks of Raven's struggle can still be seen at the Alsek River entrance — great gouges in the rock where the staff dragged, boulders displaced and scattered, the earth itself scarred by the effort of pulling the salmon from the ocean into the rivers.

title: Raven and the Beaver (Tlingit)
summary: Near a bay near Kôts!ê'L! there was a seawater pond where a beaver lived. Raven very much wanted to catch and kill this beaver, so he dug two trenches to drain the lake at low tide. After the water ran out and the beaver was visible at the bottom, Raven lowered a hook and pulled the beaver up. After killing the beaver, Raven also killed a big whale and got his people to tow it to the place where the beaver had lived. He commanded four large canoes full of people to tow the whale up the rapids through one of the canals he had made. After they labored for many days and grew tired, Raven told them to take it easy. Finally, even Raven grew tired and said, 'Turn into stone.' All did so, and to this day you can see a large island shaped like a whale with a string of four smaller islands extending from it. This Tlingit etiological myth explains a distinctive geological formation near Sitka.
source: John R. Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts (1909)
full_text:
Near a bay near Kots!ea'L! there was a seawater pond where a beaver lived. The beaver was large and old, with a tail like a leather shield and teeth that could cut through cedar. Raven very much wanted to catch and kill this beaver, for he was hungry, and the beaver was fat.

Raven dug two trenches to drain the lake at low tide. He worked through the night, his beak digging into the earth, his wings pushing the mud aside. By dawn, the trenches were complete, and when the tide went out, the water drained through them, leaving the pond empty and the beaver visible at the bottom.

Raven lowered a hook and pulled the beaver up. The beaver fought, its tail slapping against the mud, its teeth gnashing, but Raven was stronger. He killed the beaver and skinned it, roasting the meat over a fire and eating until he was full.

After killing the beaver, Raven also killed a big whale — a grey whale, enormous and slow, that had beached itself during the tide. Raven got his people to tow it to the place where the beaver had lived. He commanded four large canoes full of people to tow the whale up the rapids through one of the canals he had made.

They labored for many days and grew tired. The whale was heavy, the current was strong, and the people's arms ached. Raven told them to take it easy, but even Raven grew tired. Finally, he said, 'Turn into stone.'

All did so — the whale, the canoes, the people, the trenches, the bay itself. They turned to stone, and to this day you can see a large island shaped like a whale with a string of four smaller islands extending from it. This Tlingit etiological myth explains a distinctive geological formation near Sitka, and it reminds the people that the landscape is not simply rock and water — it is the frozen memory of ancient events.

title: Raven Turns Himself into a Woman (Tlingit)
summary: Having lost his wife Fog Woman, Raven decided to marry again so people would look after him. Rather than finding a good wife, he turned himself into a woman and married a man from the Killerwhale people. As a wife, Raven was lazy and deceitful — she stole from the Killerwhale people. Eventually she decided to kill her husband and all the Killerwhales in the village. After this destruction, the story continues with Raven visiting Fish Hawk, promising to be a good partner and share work and food. But Raven never did any work; he ate and ate while Fish Hawk provided everything. Whenever Fish Hawk grew angry, Raven flattered him, praising his wealth and generosity. Finally Fish Hawk refused to feed Raven any longer and left him to find his own food. This comic story showcases Raven's laziness, deceit, and clever manipulation, using flattery to exploit others, while also serving as a moral lesson about the consequences of trusting flatterers.
source: John R. Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts (1909); adapted by University of Alaska Fairbanks
full_text:
Having lost his wife Fog Woman, Raven decided to marry again so people would look after him. He was lazy — he hated to work, hated to fish, hated to do anything that required sustained effort. A wife would cook for him, clean for him, and keep him warm at night.

Rather than finding a good wife, he turned himself into a woman and married a man from the Killerwhale people. As a wife, Raven was lazy and deceitful. He — now she — stole from the Killerwhale people, taking food, taking blankets, taking anything that caught her eye. She ate more than anyone else and did less work than anyone else.

Eventually she decided to kill her husband and all the Killerwhales in the village. She poisoned the food, she weakened the canoes, she led the warriors into a trap. The Killerwhale people perished, and Raven, in woman's form, walked away from the destruction she had caused.

This comic story showcases Raven's laziness, deceit, and clever manipulation. Raven is not a hero — he is a trickster, and tricksters are not admirable in the conventional sense. They are clever, they are resourceful, and they always survive, but they leave a trail of destruction behind them.

The story continues with Raven visiting Fish Hawk, promising to be a good partner and share work and food. But Raven never did any work; he ate and ate while Fish Hawk provided everything. Whenever Fish Hawk grew angry, Raven flattered him, praising his wealth and generosity, telling him he was the greatest provider in the world.

Finally Fish Hawk refused to feed Raven any longer and left him to find his own food. Raven was left alone, hungry and idle, and he learned — perhaps — that even the cleverest trickster cannot live on flattery alone.

title: Raven Steals the Sun (Nuu-chah-nulth)
summary: In the Nuu-chah-nulth version of this foundational myth, there was a time before sunlight when light was kept securely in a box guarded by a great chief sometimes called the Old Fisherman. Raven wanted this light and attempted various methods to release it. He transformed himself into a floating leaf that ended up in the teacup of the great chief's daughter. She accidentally ate the leaf and in due time gave birth to Son of Raven, who was actually Raven reborn. The child was doted upon by the chief, his grandfather. Son of Raven begged to see the box of light, and after persistent pleading, the chief relented and opened the box, releasing the light. Son of Raven immediately transformed back into Raven, seized the light, and flew high into the sky. He placed the light in the sky, creating the sun that shines down on all. This myth establishes Raven as the Nuu-chah-nulth's primary culture hero and explains the origin of day and night.
source: Nuu-chah-nulth oral tradition; The Canadian Encyclopedia
full_text:
In the time before sunlight, when the world lay in darkness and the people stumbled through their days half-blind, light existed — but it was hoarded. A great chief, sometimes called the Old Fisherman, kept all the light of the universe locked in a nested set of five boxes, each smaller than the last, each more tightly sealed. The chief guarded his treasure jealously, letting no light escape, keeping the world in shadow.

Raven wanted that light. Not for altruistic reasons — Raven was never altruistic — but because he was tired of the dark. He wanted to see where he was walking. He wanted to find the salmon streams. He wanted to examine the faces of the people he tricked. Darkness was inconvenient for a trickster.

So Raven devised a plan — the kind of plan that only Raven could devise, involving deception, manipulation, and the exploitation of a grandfather's love.

Raven transformed himself into a hemlock needle — tiny, green, nearly invisible — and dropped into the river where the chief's daughter came each morning to draw water. The daughter filled her cedar bucket, carried it home, and poured it into the family's drinking vessel. The needle floated on the surface, glinting in the dim light.

When the daughter drank, she swallowed the needle. And in time, as such things happen in the stories of the beginning, she gave birth to a child — a boy with dark eyes and a cry like a raven's call. The old chief, her father, was overjoyed. He had no grandchildren, and this child was precious to him beyond measure.

The child grew with supernatural speed, and the chief doted on him, giving him everything he asked for. And what the child asked for, relentlessly, persistently, with the inexhaustible energy of a baby who knows exactly what he wants, was the boxes.

"Grandfather, I want to see the boxes."

"No, grandchild. You must not touch them."

"Grandfather, please. Just one box. Just to hold."

"No, grandchild."

The child cried. He cried all night, his wail rising through the cedar walls of the house, shaking the roof beams. He cried all day, his tears running down his face in rivers, his fists clenched, his voice hoarse but unrelenting. The chief could not sleep. The household could not function. The daughter begged her father to give the child what he wanted.

At last, worn down by the crying, the chief relented. He brought out the first box — the largest — and opened it.

The stars burst free. They flew from the box like sparks from a fire, swirling upward, embedding themselves in the dark sky. The world flickered with faint light — the first light it had known.

But the child wanted more. He cried for the second box, and the chief opened it, and the moon rose out of it like a silver fish jumping from the water, climbing the sky, casting its pale glow over the world.

The child wanted the third box. The chief opened it, and the northern lights — the aurora — spilled out, painting the sky with curtains of green and violet and white, rippling like fabric in a wind that blew from the edge of the world.

Now the child stopped crying. He held the remaining two boxes — the smallest, the most tightly sealed — and the chief watched with growing unease, for he knew that the last box held the greatest treasure.

The child fumbled with the seals. The chief tried to stop him, but it was too late. The child tore open the final box, and the sun — the blazing, golden, world-illuminating sun — erupted from his hands. In the same instant, the child transformed. His body stretched and darkened, his arms became wings, his beak lengthened, and he was Raven again — not a baby, not a trickster in disguise, but Raven in his true form, black as the night he was about to destroy.

Raven seized the sun in his beak and flew. He flew up, up, past the smoke hole of the chief's house, past the clouds, past the stars he had released, into the sky itself. And there he released the sun, placing it in the highest reaches of the heavens, where it blazed forth and flooded the world with daylight.

The darkness was over. The world could see.

This myth — told by the Nuu-chah-nulth and by peoples across the Pacific Northwest in variations that differ in detail but agree in essence — establishes Raven as the primary culture hero and explains the origin of day and night. Light, in the Nuu-chah-nulth understanding, was not given freely by the gods. It was stolen, tricked, wrested from the clutches of those who would hoard it. And it was Raven — selfish, clever, insatiable Raven — who brought it to the people, not because he loved them, but because he wanted to see where he was going.

title: Raven Annoys Octopus (Nuu-chah-nulth)
summary: One morning as the tide went out, the old people came to sit and watch the ocean. They saw a woman walking along the beach with her hair long and strung into eight braids — she was Octopus, carrying a digging stick to look for clams. She sat down on a rock and began to dig. Soon another person came along the beach, tall with glossy black hair — it was Raven. The old people predicted he would bother Octopus, and they knew it was not a good idea. Raven walked right down to the rock where Octopus sat and began bothering her. He teased and pestered her while she tried to dig for clams. The story serves as a humorous cautionary tale about respecting others' boundaries and not interfering with people who are working. Raven's persistent meddling backfires, teaching him (and the listener) that pestering others leads to unpleasant consequences. The Nuu-chah-nulth version emphasizes Raven's trickster nature and his tendency to interfere in others' affairs.
full_text:
One morning as the tide went out, the old people came to sit on the warm rocks and watch the ocean. This was what old people did in the villages along the coast — they watched the water, they talked about the weather, they remembered things that had happened when the world was younger. The tide was low, and the rocks were dry, and the morning sun was warm on their faces.

They saw a woman walking along the beach. She was alone, and she moved with a steady, purposeful stride. Her hair was long — very long — strung into eight braids that hung down her back like dark ropes. She carried a digging stick in one hand, and she was looking for clams.

The old people recognized her. She was Octopus — not a human woman but a spirit-being who took human form when she came to the shore to dig for clams. Her eight braids were the eight arms she would reveal if she chose to, and her digging stick was the tool she used to pry clams from the sand.

Octopus sat down on a flat rock near the water's edge and began to dig. She worked slowly, methodically, pushing the stick into the wet sand, prying up the surface, finding the clams beneath. She was absorbed in her work, and she did not notice the figure approaching along the beach.

He was tall, with glossy black hair that caught the light like oil on water. His step was light, almost dancing, and there was a smirk on his face that the old people recognized immediately.

"That's Raven," one of them muttered. "And he's going to bother her."

The others nodded. They had seen this before. Raven could not leave anyone in peace. If someone was working, Raven wanted to interfere. If someone was happy, Raven wanted to make them unhappy. If someone was sitting quietly on a rock digging for clams, Raven wanted to make their life miserable.

Raven walked right down to the rock where Octopus sat. He did not announce himself. He did not greet her with the proper words. He simply walked up and began talking — nonsense, mostly, the kind of restless, probing chatter that Raven used when he was bored and looking for amusement.

"What are you doing?" he asked, though it was obvious.

"Digging clams," Octopus said, not looking up.

"Why?"

"To eat."

"What kind of clams?"

"The kind that live in the sand."

"I know that. But what kind?"

Octopus ignored him. She dug another clam from the sand and placed it in her basket.

Raven leaned closer. He peered into the hole she had dug. He nudged her arm with his elbow. He picked up a handful of sand and let it trickle through his fingers. He made comments about her technique, her braids, her stick, the quality of the clams, the state of the tide.

The old people on the rocks shook their heads. They knew how this would end. Raven never learned. He never understood that bothering people was wrong, or that persistence in irritation was not the same as charm. He would keep pestering Octopus until she had enough, and then there would be consequences.

The story — told along the coast from village to village, generation to generation — is a humorous cautionary tale about respecting others' boundaries and not interfering with people who are working. Raven's persistent meddling backfires, as it always does, teaching him and the listener that pestering others leads to unpleasant consequences. The Nuu-chah-nulth version emphasizes Raven's trickster nature and his tendency to interfere in others' affairs, even when those affairs are none of his business.

title: Raven Becomes Voracious (Tsimshian)
summary: This Tsimshian myth explains how Raven acquired his insatiable appetite and voracious nature. Before this story, Raven was not known for his hunger. Through a series of events involving trickery, greed, and supernatural encounters, Raven's appetite grew beyond all bounds. He began devouring everything in sight, from salmon to berries, from seal meat to olachen grease. His hunger became so legendary that it defined his character. The story serves as an etiological myth explaining why ravens and crows are scavengers who eat constantly and are always hungry. It also carries a moral lesson about the dangers of greed and insatiable desire. Raven's voraciousness is both a humorous trait — he is constantly scheming to get food — and a serious warning about what happens when consumption becomes uncontrolled. The story is part of the larger Tsimshian Raven cycle that portrays Txamsem as both a world-creating culture hero and a deeply flawed, comic figure.
source: Franz Boas, Tsimshian Mythology; Tsimshian oral tradition
full_text:
This Tsimshian myth explains how Raven acquired his insatiable appetite and voracious nature. Before this story, Raven was not known for his hunger. He was clever, yes, and mischievous, but he was not the creature of endless appetite that he would become.

Through a series of events involving trickery, greed, and supernatural encounters, Raven's appetite grew beyond all bounds. He began devouring everything in sight, from salmon to berries, from seal meat to olachen grease. His hunger became so legendary that it defined his character — he was no longer simply Raven the trickster; he was Raven the hungry, Raven the devourer, Raven who could never be satisfied.

The story serves as an etiological myth explaining why ravens and crows are scavengers who eat constantly and are always hungry. The birds peck at garbage, at carcasses, at anything that might contain a morsel of food, because Raven's hunger lives in them — an eternal, unsatisfiable need that drives them to eat and eat and eat.

It also carries a moral lesson about the dangers of greed and insatiable desire. Raven's voraciousness is both a humorous trait — he is constantly scheming to get food, his plans becoming more elaborate and more ridiculous with each attempt — and a serious warning about what happens when consumption becomes uncontrolled.

The story is part of the larger Tsimshian Raven cycle that portrays Txamsem as both a world-creating culture hero and a deeply flawed, comic figure. Raven brings gifts to the people — light, fish, fire — but he also brings trouble, and his hunger is the source of both his generosity and his destruction.

title: Raven Brings Light (Nuxalk - Qwaxw)
summary: In the beginning, when the world was covered in darkness, the people were in constant sadness and prayed to the Creator Alhkw'ntam for light. Alhkw'ntam held the sun in a box in his longhouse in Nusmata (the land above) and let no one see it. The Four Carpenters who made the world were sitting around a fire when the eldest, Yulm, grabbed a piece of charcoal and shook it in his hands. When he opened his hands, it was a bird. The second Carpenter made its wings, the third made its eyes, and the youngest gave it life. They asked the bird to say its name and it flew into the sky crying 'Qwaxw, qwaxw, qwaxw!' — they named it Qwaxw, Raven. The people begged Raven to get the light. He flew to Nusmata and observed Alhkw'ntam's granddaughter Skimina. He transformed into eagle down, then a hemlock needle, but she blew him away. Finally he muddied her drinking water, and she drank him in. She became pregnant and Raven was born as her child. Raven cried for the box holding the light until Alhkw'ntam gave in. Raven broke the globe against the wall, and light leaked through the smoke vent to become the sun, stars, and moon. The people were no longer sad.
source: Nuxalk oral tradition; Nuxalk Nation official website; Franz Boas, The Mythology of the Bella Coola Indians
full_text:
In the beginning, when the world was covered in darkness, the people were in constant sadness and prayed to the Creator Alhkw'ntam for light. Alhkw'ntam held the sun in a box in his longhouse in Nusmata, the land above, and let no one see it. The box was locked, and the key was hidden, and the people's prayers went unanswered.

The Four Carpenters who made the world were sitting around a fire when the eldest, Yulm, grabbed a piece of charcoal and shook it in his hands. When he opened his hands, it was a bird — small, black, and ordinary. The second Carpenter made its wings, the third made its eyes, and the youngest gave it life.

They asked the bird to say its name and it flew into the sky crying 'Qwaxw, qwaxw, qwaxw!' — they named it Qwaxw, Raven.

The people begged Raven to get the light. He flew to Nusmata and observed Alhkw'ntam's granddaughter Skimina. He transformed into eagle down — soft, white, drifting — but she blew him away. Then he transformed into a hemlock needle — small, sharp, ordinary — but she blew him away again. Finally he muddied her drinking water, and she drank him in.

She became pregnant and Raven was born as her child. The child cried incessantly, his voice high and piercing, until Alhkw'ntam gave in and offered him the box holding the light. Raven broke the globe against the wall, and light leaked through the smoke vent to become the sun, stars, and moon.

The people were no longer sad. They looked up and saw the light — warm, bright, beautiful — and they celebrated the gift that Raven had brought them.

This myth emphasizes the cooperative work of the carpenters, Raven's role as mediator between heaven and earth, and the Nuxalk belief that the sun is a living being with whom they maintain a spiritual relationship.

title: Robin and Blue-Jay (Chinook)
summary: Blue Jay and Robin, two brothers, were hungry. Blue Jay called a large fish (the sleeper) to come ashore through trickery and speared it. When they returned home, Robin asked for the tail, breast, and head, making Blue Jay angry. He said that the Q!têê'nse (a supernatural monster) would eat the fish instead. Robin cried and left. Blue Jay softened and called his brother back, giving him all the choice parts. Later, Blue Jay dreamed that people were sending for him to cure a sick person. Blue Jay and Robin journeyed to cure a duck who was choking, receiving payment of a lake's worth of roots. Next they cured a wolf girl who was choking on an elk's kneecap, receiving two canoes full of meat and grease. But Blue Jay's arrogance and greed in demanding excessive payment led to consequences. The story demonstrates the Chinook trickster cycle's typical structure: Blue Jay is boastful and selfish but ultimately provides for his family through his supernatural curing abilities, while long-suffering Robin represents patience and humility.
source: Franz Boas, Chinook Texts (1894); Chinook oral tradition from Charles Cultee
full_text:
Blue Jay and Robin, two brothers, were hungry. They had not eaten in two days, and their stomachs growled like empty caves. They stood at the edge of the creek, watching the water flow, and Blue Jay said, "I will get us food."

Robin looked at him doubtfully. Blue Jay was always saying he would do things, and he often did them, but he also often got them into trouble.

Blue Jay called to the water. He made a sound — a low, rhythmic pulsing that traveled through the surface of the creek like a heartbeat. It was the sound that the sleeper fish makes when it rests on the bottom, and in time a large fish — fat and slow — rose from the depths and drifted toward the shore.

Blue Jay speared it. It was a good fish, heavy and silver, enough to feed them both.

They carried it home and built a fire. Robin, who was younger and more eager, reached for the fish and asked for the tail. Then he asked for the breast. Then he asked for the head.

Blue Jay's feathers ruffled. "You want everything," he said. "You want the best parts. What about me?"

"I'm hungry," Robin said.

"The Q!təə'nse will eat the fish instead," Blue Jay said, naming the great supernatural monster that lived in the deep forest, the one that ate everything it found. It was a cruel thing to say, and Blue Jay knew it, but he was angry.

Robin cried. He cried loudly, as younger brothers do, and then he left. He walked away from the fire, away from the fish, away from Blue Jay, and disappeared into the forest.

Blue Jay sat by the fire for a long time, eating the fish alone. But as the fire burned low and the night grew cold, his anger cooled too, and his stomach was full, and he began to feel the particular emptiness that comes from having eaten well while someone you love goes hungry.

He called Robin back. "Come eat," he said, and his voice was soft. Robin returned, and Blue Jay gave him all the choice parts — the tail, the breast, the head — everything he had kept for himself.

Later, Blue Jay dreamed that people were sending for him to cure a sick person. He and Robin journeyed to the village where the sick one lay — a duck who was choking on a bone. Blue Jay removed the bone and cured the duck, and the people rewarded him with a lake's worth of roots.

Next they cured a wolf girl who was choking on an elk's kneecap, receiving two canoes full of meat and grease.

But Blue Jay's arrogance and greed in demanding excessive payment led to consequences. The people grew tired of his boasting, his demands, his insistence that he was the greatest healer in the world. They chased him away, and Blue Jay flew off, still boasting, still insisting, still unable to see himself as others saw him.

The Chinook trickster cycle's typical structure is on display here: Blue Jay is boastful and selfish but ultimately provides for his family through his supernatural curing abilities, while long-suffering Robin represents patience and humility. The brothers need each other — Blue Jay's power and Robin's goodness — and neither is complete without the other.

title: The Rabbit Trickster of the Kongo
summary: Among the Kongo, the rabbit (sometimes called Nsumunu) is the greatest of all tricksters, smaller than nearly every other creature but cleverer than them all. In the most famous tale, Rabbit grew tired of drinking from muddy puddles while the great elephant and hippo drank from the clear river. Rabbit challenged them to a tug-of-war, tying one end of a rope around elephant's trunk and the other around hippo's tail, then hiding in the bushes and shouting 'Pull!' The two giants pulled against each other for hours, each believing Rabbit was on the other end, until they collapsed from exhaustion. Rabbit then calmly walked to the river and drank his fill. Chief Leopard, furious at Rabbit's trickery, tried to catch and eat him, but Rabbit always escaped — hiding in thorn bushes Leopard could not enter or using honey to glue Leopard's paws together. The Rabbit stories teach that intelligence and wit will always overcome brute force.
source: Kongo oral tradition, Central African folklore
moral: Small and clever can triumph over large and strong through wit and patience.
full_text:
Rabbit was tired of muddy puddles. Every other animal drank from the clear river — Elephant with his great trunk, Hippo with his wide mouth, even the small birds dipped their beaks in the flowing water. But Rabbit, who was the smallest and weakest, could only drink from puddles that stank of mud and mosquito larvae.

"I will fix this," Rabbit said to himself. He tied one end of a long vine to Elephant's trunk and the other end to Hippo's tail. Then he hid in the bushes and shouted:

"Pull!"

Elephant pulled east. Hippo pulled west. Each believed Rabbit was on the other end, and each was determined not to be outdone. They pulled and pulled, their feet gouging the earth, their breath coming in great gasps. The vine stretched. The ground shook.

Rabbit watched from the bushes, eating a stalk of grass. Hours passed. The sun climbed. Elephant's trunk ached. Hippo's tail throbbed. Neither would give up.

By evening, both had collapsed from exhaustion. The vine lay limp between them. Rabbit walked calmly to the river, knelt at the bank, and drank his fill.

"What happened?" Elephant asked, lifting his head.

"Rabbit tricked us," Hippo said, licking his sore tail.

But Rabbit was already gone, his belly full, his ears twitching with satisfaction.

Chief Leopard was furious when he heard the story. He was the king of the forest, and Rabbit's trickery was an insult to his authority. He set a trap — a pit hidden beneath leaves, baited with Rabbit's favorite food.

Rabbit found the pit. He studied it for a moment, then called out: "Leopard! I have caught something wonderful! Come see!"

Leopard ran to the pit and looked in — and fell in himself. Rabbit covered the pit with branches and walked away.

Leopard scratched and clawed his way out, but by the time he emerged, Rabbit was nowhere to be found. He had hidden in a thorn bush, where Leopard's great paws could not reach him.

The Kongo tell these stories to teach their children that intelligence and wit will always overcome brute force. Rabbit is small, but he is never defeated. Leopard is mighty, but he is never victorious. And in the animal kingdom, as in the human world, the clever survive while the strong merely endure.

title: Ruwa and the Sacred Mountain Kilimanjaro
summary: Ruwa, the supreme god of the Chaga people, dwells upon the snow-capped peak of Kilimanjaro, the highest mountain in Africa. According to Chaga cosmology, Ruwa is associated with the sun and resides in the sky alongside his consort, the moon. From his celestial throne on Kibo peak, Ruwa watches over the Chaga people and all creation. The mountain is not merely a mountain but the physical manifestation of Ruwa's presence on earth — its glaciers are his crown, its forests his garments, its rivers his blessings flowing down to nourish the people. Sacrifices to Ruwa are performed at high noon, when the sun is at its zenith, in sacred groves on the mountain's slopes. The spirits of Chaga chiefs (Mangi) who have passed away join Ruwa on the mountain, interceding for their descendants. The Chaga believe that the mountain's glaciers will never fully melt, for as long as they remain, Ruwa's protection endures. Kilimanjaro is thus the sacred center of Chaga spiritual life.
source: Chaga oral tradition, Charles Dundas 'Kilimanjaro and Its People'
moral: The divine presence manifests in the most magnificent features of the natural world.
full_text:
Ruwa was the Chaga name for the supreme god — the possessor of the mountain, the keeper of the snow, the one who dwelt on the highest peak of Kilimanjaro.

The Chaga believed that Ruwa's home was the ice cap that crowned the mountain — a dome of white that gleamed in the equatorial sun. From that height, Ruwa watched over the Chaga people, sending rain when they were good and drought when they were not.

The Chaga did not worship Ruwa directly. He was too vast, too distant, too cosmic for human rituals. Instead, they honored him through the natural world — through the forests that covered the mountain's slopes, through the rivers that flowed from its glaciers, through the soil that sustained their crops.

When the Chaga needed Ruwa's help, they climbed to a sacred site on the mountain — a clearing, a cave, a rock formation that marked the boundary between the human world and the divine. There, they offered sacrifices: a white goat, a calabash of beer, a string of beads. They raised their hands toward the snow-capped peak and spoke their prayers.

Ruwa answered through signs. A clear sky meant his favor. A cloud over the peak meant his concern. A storm meant his wrath. And the snow — the eternal snow — was his promise that the mountain, and the people who lived on it, would endure.

The Chaga say that Ruwa created Kilimanjaro as a pillar to hold up the sky. When the sky threatened to fall, Ruwa built the mountain higher, adding snow and ice to its peak to anchor it in place. The mountain is not merely a geological formation; it is a divine architecture, a bridge between earth and heaven.

To this day, the Chaga people look up at Kilimanjaro and see Ruwa's face in the snow. They see the god who made their world, who watches over their fields, who sends the rain. And they remember that the mountain is not just a mountain — it is a throne.

title: The Rain Princess of the Sotho
summary: Sotho oral tradition tells of a rain princess who possessed the power to control the weather and bring fertility to the land. In times of drought, the Sotho people would perform ceremonies to honor the rain princess and her connection to Modimo, the supreme god. The princess was both a spiritual figure and a political leader, embodying the link between the people and the divine forces that governed their agricultural existence. Her ability to summon rain was tied to strict ritual observances, and any breach of tradition could result in devastating drought. This figure reflects the central importance of rain in the semi-arid highlands of southern Africa, where water determined survival.
full_text:
The Rain Princess was the daughter of the king of the Sotho — a woman of extraordinary beauty and supernatural power. She could call rain with a song, bring clouds with a gesture, and stop the rain with a clap of her hands.

The king loved his daughter more than anything in the world. But he feared losing her. When suitors came to ask for her hand, the king set impossible tasks: "Bring me a lion's mane," he said. "Bring me a stone that sings. Bring me water that flows uphill."

No suitor could complete the tasks. The Rain Princess remained unmarried, growing more beautiful and more powerful with each passing year.

But the Rain Princess was lonely. She wanted to marry, to have children, to live a life beyond the palace walls. She prayed to the ancestors for help.

The ancestors sent a young man — a herder with no cattle and no family, but with a heart as pure as mountain water. He came to the palace and asked the king for the Rain Princess's hand.

The king set the impossible tasks. The herder completed them all — not through strength or magic, but through kindness. He asked the animals for help, and they helped. He asked the plants for help, and they helped. He asked the spirits for help, and they helped.

The king could not refuse. The Rain Princess married the herder, and together they brought rain to the land. The crops grew. The rivers filled. The people prospered.

The Sotho say that the Rain Princess is the spirit of the rain itself — beautiful, powerful, and free. She cannot be captured or controlled. She can only be loved.

title: Rangi and Papa: The Separation of Sky and Earth
summary: In the beginning, Ranginui (Sky Father) and Papatuanuku (Earth Mother) lay locked in a tight embrace, leaving their children trapped in darkness between them. The children grew weary of the cramped darkness and debated how to gain freedom. Tane Mahuta, god of forests, proposed separating their parents. While Tawhirimatea opposed, Tane lay on his back and pushed upward with his feet, forcing Rangi upward and thrusting Papa down. Thus light entered the world. Tawhirimatea, enraged, joined his father in the sky and sent storms against his siblings, beginning the eternal conflict between wind, forest, sea, and land.
full_text:
In the time before time, Rangi the Sky Father lay pressed close against Papa the Earth Mother, and between them they held all their children in a dark, warm embrace. Their children—the gods of forest, sea, wind, and war—existed in cramped blackness, unable to move or see. Among them were Tane Mahuta, god of forests and birds; Tangaroa, god of the sea; Tawhiri Matea, god of winds and storms; Haumia-tiketike, god of wild food; Rongo, god of cultivated food and peace; and Tu, god of war. Each child longed for space, for light, for the world above.

The brothers gathered in council to discuss their plight. "Let us push our parents apart," said Tu, "so that we may live in the light." But the brothers disagreed on how far to separate them. Tane wanted gentle light and soft rain for the forests. Tangaroa wanted the sky far enough that tides would ebb and flow. Tawhiri wanted to remain close to his mother Rangi, to rage and weep against her body as storms.

Tane Mahuta pressed his great strength against Papa while Rangi pleaded with them to stop. When Tane finally thrust the Sky Father upward with his mighty back, light flooded the world for the first time. Rangi wept for her lost children, and her tears fell as rain upon the new land. Tawhiri, refusing to leave his mother, flew upward with her and became the storms that still rage between sky and earth. The other brothers settled on Papa's body and became the forests, the seas, the fertile ground, and the wild creatures.

Thus the world was born from separation and grief. The Maori say that even now, when the mist rises from the mountains on still mornings, it is Rangi's breath reaching down to embrace Papa once more, a love that separation could never fully destroy.

title: The Rainbow Serpent and the Creation of the Land
summary: The Rainbow Serpent (known by many names across Australia including Julunggul, Kunmanggur, and Wagyl) is one of the most widespread and significant creator beings in Aboriginal Australian mythology. In the Dreamtime, the great Rainbow Serpent traveled across the land, creating rivers, gorges, mountains, and waterholes as she moved. She emerged from the ground after sleeping beneath the earth and her journey shaped the landscape into its present form. She gave life to plants and animals, established the laws for human society, and taught the people how to live properly. The Rainbow Serpent is associated with rain, water, fertility, and regeneration, but also with danger. She can punish those who break the law with floods, lightning, and storms. The Rainbow Serpent remains present in deep waterholes and continues to protect sacred sites.
full_text:
The Rainbow Serpent, known by many names across Australia including Julunggul, Kunmanggur, and Wagyl, is one of the most widespread and significant creator beings in Aboriginal Australian mythology. In the Dreamtime, the great Rainbow Serpent traveled across the land, creating rivers, gorges, mountains, and waterholes as she moved.

She emerged from the ground after sleeping beneath the earth for millennia, her great body covered in scales that shimmered with every color of the rainbow. As she slithered across the landscape, her massive body carved riverbeds, her passage created valleys, and her coils formed mountains. She was the sculptor of the continent, shaping Australia with the slow, patient power of geological time.

She gave life to plants and animals, establishing the laws for human society and teaching the people how to live properly. She showed them which plants were food and which were poison, which animals could be hunted and which were sacred. She established the systems of totem and kinship that governed Aboriginal society, connecting every person to the land, to the animals, and to the ancestors.

The Rainbow Serpent is associated with rain, water, fertility, and regeneration, but also with danger. She can punish those who break the law with floods, lightning, and storms. When the rivers flood, it is the Rainbow Serpent's anger. When the rains come gently, it is her blessing.

The Rainbow Serpent remains present in deep waterholes and continues to protect sacred sites across Australia. The waterholes are her resting places, and they are treated with the utmost respect. To pollute a waterhole is to offend the Rainbow Serpent, and the consequences are severe.

The people of Australia say that the Rainbow Serpent is the oldest living being in the world—older than the mountains, older than the rivers, older than the stars. She was there at the beginning of the Dreamtime, and she will be there at the end. Her power is the power of water, the source of all life, and her story is the story of Australia itself.

title: The Raven and the Whale
summary: A Chukchi story from the Kuutkh cycle describing how the Raven creator interacted with the primordial whale. In this tale, Kuutkh encounters a giant whale that threatens the newly created world. Through a combination of trickery and negotiation, the Raven convinces the whale to accept boundaries for its territory, establishing the separation of sea and land. The whale becomes the ruler of the ocean while the Raven takes dominion over the land and sky. This myth establishes the cosmological order of the Chukchi world, explaining why whales remain in the ocean and ravens on land. It reflects the importance of both reindeer herding (inland) and sea mammal hunting (coastal) in Chukchi subsistence.
full_text:
The whale was ancient before the world had a name. It lived in the primordial ocean — the black water that covered everything before Kuutkh the Raven created the land — and it was vast, its body as large as an island, its mouth wide enough to swallow the sun. When Kuutkh began creating, pulling up mud and shaping mountains and scratching rivers into the earth, the whale stirred. The land was growing, spreading, encroaching on the ocean's territory, and the whale did not like it.

The whale rose from the deep. Its back broke the surface like a new continent, and the spray from its blowhole formed clouds that rained for days. It looked at the land Kuutkh had made and decided to destroy it. It opened its mouth and began to swallow — taking in coastlines, cliffs, beaches, anything that stood between the water and the sky.

Kuutkh saw what was happening and flew down to confront the whale. He landed on its head — a mountain of wet, glistening flesh — and said: "You cannot eat the world. If you eat the world, there will be nothing left for either of us."

The whale considered this. It was not a stupid creature; it was merely old, and old things are suspicious of change. "Why should I share?" the whale said. "The water was mine before you began making your land."

"Because if you eat the land, the fish will have nowhere to spawn," Kuutkh said. "The seals will have nowhere to rest. The birds will have nowhere to nest. You will have the water, but the water will be empty."

The whale was silent for a long time. The ocean moved around its body, and the wind blew across its wet skin. At last, it spoke: "Very well. I will accept boundaries. I will keep the water, and you will keep the land. But tell your people this: the ocean is mine, and everything in it answers to me. If they take fish, they must ask permission. If they hunt seals, they must make offerings. If they anger me, I will take back what is mine."

Kuutkh agreed. The whale sank back into the ocean, and the boundary between land and water was established — a boundary that has held ever since. The maritime Chukchi, who hunt sea mammals along the coast, still make offerings to the whale spirits before embarking on their hunts. The inland Chukchi, who herd reindeer, make offerings to the spirits of the land. Both traditions stem from the agreement between Kuutkh and the whale — the ancient compact that divided the world into its proper spheres.

title: Raven the Creator (Nivkh Tradition)
summary: The Nivkh creation myth centered on the Raven, a central figure shared with neighboring Chukchi and Koryak traditions. In Nivkh mythology, the Raven (known as Kurka or similar names) created the world by diving into the primordial sea and bringing up earth on his beak. He shaped the land of Sakhalin Island and the Amur River estuary, and then created human beings from clay mixed with his own feathers. The Raven is both creator and trickster who taught the Nivkh people how to fish, build canoes, and conduct the sacred bear ceremony. The myths also explain how the Raven brought the sun and moon into the sky by stealing them from a powerful spirit. Nivkh folklore was first systematically recorded by Bronisław Piłsudski and later by Vladimir Sangi.
full_text:
In the time before time, when the world was nothing but a vast and formless sea, the Raven — called Kurka by the Nivkh people — flew above the endless water and saw that there was nowhere to land. The wind was cold. The darkness was complete. And the Raven, who was both creator and trickster, decided that this would not do.

He dove beneath the waves, plunging into the black water until his feathers burned and his lungs ached. He scooped up a beakful of mud and struggled back to the surface, where he spat the mud into the air. It spread, and spread, and spread — becoming the land of Sakhalin Island, the Amur River estuary, and all the shores where the Nivkh would one day make their home.

Then the Raven shaped human beings from clay, mixing in his own feathers to give them warmth and cunning. He taught them to fish the rivers, to build their skin canoes, and to perform the sacred bear ceremony that would keep the spirits of the forest appeased. But the Raven's greatest feat was bringing light itself — he stole the sun and moon from a powerful spirit who had hoarded them, and hurled them into the sky, where they burned forever after.

The Nivkh people remember the Raven not as a distant, perfect god but as a vivid, flawed character — generous and selfish, wise and foolish, creative and destructive by turns. His stories are told around the fire in winter, when the darkness presses close and the old ones say that Kurka himself might be listening, crouched in the corner of the hut, cocking his head to hear what they say about him.

title: Roro Jonggrang and the Legend of Prambanan Temple
summary: A Javanese legend explaining the origin of Prambanan Temple. Bandung Bondowoso, a powerful prince with supernatural abilities and an army of invisible genies, fell in love with Princess Roro Jonggrang. When she rejected his proposal, he attacked her father's kingdom and conquered it. Forced to consider marriage, Roro Jonggrang set an impossible condition: Bandung must build 1,000 temples in one night. Using his supernatural army, he nearly completed the task. Desperate, Roro Jonggrang ordered her maids to light fires and pound rice, tricking the spirits into thinking dawn had arrived. Enraged by the deception, Bandung cursed Roro Jonggrang, transforming her into the 1,000th statue — which remains at Prambanan to this day.
notes: Explains the origin of Prambanan Temple, a UNESCO World Heritage site in Central Java.
moral: True honor lives on in stories passed down through generations.
full_text:
Bandung Bondowoso was a prince of supernatural power — a man who could command the invisible, who could raise armies of jinn and earth spirits with a single chant. His armies were not made of flesh and bone but of shadow and flame, and they obeyed his every command. When he rode to war, the ground trembled. When he spoke, the wind stopped. When he loved, the earth itself seemed to lean toward him.

He loved Roro Jonggrang. She was the daughter of the king of Prambanan, and she was beautiful in the way that a temple is beautiful — precise, symmetrical, luminous. Bandung Bondowoso conquered her father's kingdom with his supernatural army and declared that Roro Jonggrang would be his bride.

Roro Jonggrang refused. She could not refuse outright — he had conquered her kingdom, and defiance meant death. So she set a condition: Bandung must build one thousand temples in a single night. If he succeeded, she would marry him. If he failed, he would release her and leave.

Bandung Bondowoso accepted. At midnight, he summoned the spirits of the earth. They came in a horde — thousands of jinn, rising from the ground like smoke, their eyes burning, their hands clawed. They worked through the night, stone by stone, temple by temple. Nine hundred and ninety-nine temples rose from the earth, each one more beautiful than the last, their spires reaching toward the stars.

Roro Jonggrang saw that Bandung would succeed. She ordered her maids to light fires and pound rice — the clanging of the mortars, the smoke from the fires, the light from the torches. The spirits of the dawn — the roosters, the light-bringers — saw the glow and thought the sun was rising. They fled. The nine hundred and ninety-ninth temple remained incomplete.

Bandung Bondowoso was enraged. He turned on Roro Jonggrang and cursed her. "You deceived me," he said, "and now you will pay the price." His curse struck, and Roro Jonggrang's body turned to stone. She became the thousandth statue — the final element of the temple complex — and she remains there still, frozen in stone at Prambanan, a princess who tried to outwit a sorcerer and lost.

title: The Riri Yaksha and Suniyam Sorcery Legends
summary: The Riri Yaksha (Blood Demon) is one of the most feared demonic figures in Sinhalese folklore, central to the Bali and Tovil exorcism traditions. According to legend, Riri Yaksha was born from the blood of a slain demon, possessing enormous power and an insatiable thirst. The Suniyam demon, associated with sorcery and black magic, is believed to be a Yaksha who once served the god Vishnu but was cursed. Sinhalese folklore describes Suniyam as the chief of all demons governing disease, misfortune, and madness. The Tovil ritual, involving elaborate masks, drumming, and dances, is performed to exorcise these malevolent spirits. These Yakshas are neither purely evil nor good — they can be both disease-bringers and protectors when properly propitiated.
source: Sinhalese Tovil exorcism traditions, Gananath Obeyesekere studies
moral: Wisdom and wit prevail where strength alone cannot
full_text:
The Riri Yaksha was born from blood. When the great demon was slain by the gods, his blood fell to the earth and congealed into a new entity — a being of pure malice, whose very existence was an act of violence. He was the Blood Demon, the Red Spirit, the one who fed on the life force of the living and left them drained and hollow.

He was not alone. The Suniyam demon, who had once served the god Vishnu, was cursed for his pride and cast down into the realm of spirits. He became the chief of sorcery, the master of black magic, the demon who whispered in the ears of the wicked and taught them the spells that could kill without evidence, destroy without trace.

Together, the Riri Yaksha and Suniyam formed the twin terrors of Sinhalese folklore. The Riri Yaksha brought disease — the sudden fevers, the unexplained bleeding, the wasting sicknesses that left villages empty. Suniyam brought misfortune — the failed crops, the lost livestock, the madness that crept into the minds of the unwary.

The Tovil ritual was their antidote. The exorcist, masked and drumming, entered the realm of the spirits and confronted the demons in their own territory. He danced with them, sang with them, offered them food and tribute. But beneath the performance was a negotiation — a barter between the human world and the spirit world, in which the demons were persuaded to leave in exchange for offerings.

The Yakshas were neither purely evil nor purely good. They were spirits of necessity — forces that had to be acknowledged, respected, and appeased. To ignore them was to invite catastrophe. To honor them was to ensure survival. The boundary between the human and the demonic was not a wall but a membrane, and the Tovil ritual was the art of permeating that membrane without being consumed.

title: Rannamaari: The Sea Demon That Demanded Sacrifice
summary: In pre-Islamic Maldives, a terrible sea demon called Rannamaari rose from the ocean each month to demand a sacrificed virgin. The girls were dressed in fine clothes and left alone in a Buddhist temple on the eastern seafront of Malé; by dawn, they were found violated and dead. This terror continued until a Maghrebi Muslim traveler, Abu'l-Barakat al-Barbari (or Yusuf al-Tabrezi from Tabriz, Iran), volunteered to take the girl's place. He spent the night reciting the Quran, and when the demon appeared, the holy verses caused it to flee into the sea, never to return. The king, identified as Dhovemi, converted to Islam and took the name Sultan Muhammad ibn Abdullah in 1153 CE, and the Maldives became a Muslim nation. Historians note parallels with Buddhist tantric rituals, and folklorist Xavier Romero-Frias traces the name Rannamaari to a South Indian goddess.
source: Ibn Battuta travelogue (14th century), Isdhoo Loamaafaanu copper plates, Xavier Romero-Frias research
moral: Wisdom and wit prevail where strength alone cannot
full_text:
The demon rose from the water at the new moon, when the sky was black and the sea was a void without horizon or boundary. It was massive — a shape of darkness and hunger that emerged from the surf like a nightmare made flesh. Every month it came, and every month it demanded a virgin. The girl was dressed in fine clothes, adorned with gold and flowers, and left alone in the Buddhist temple on the eastern seafront of Malé. By morning, she was found violated and dead.

Abu'l-Barakat al-Barbari volunteered. He was a traveler from the Maghreb, a scholar of the Quran, a man who had seen enough of the world to know that evil does not retreat before swords but before faith. He sat in the temple with the Quran in his lap and read. The words filled the stone chamber with a light that was not physical — a radiance that pushed back the darkness and made the air vibrate with power.

The demon appeared. It was massive, its body filling the doorway, its eyes like holes in the darkness. Abu'l-Barakat read on. The Quranic verses struck the demon like blows — each word a hammer, each syllable a blade. The demon screamed and fled into the sea, never to return.

The king, Dhovemi, converted to Islam. He took the name Sultan Muhammad ibn Abdullah, and the Maldives became a Muslim nation. The Buddhist temple was replaced by a mosque — the Hukuru Miskiiy, the Friday Mosque, built from coral stone that still stands in Malé. The demon was defeated, but the story of Rannamaari endures, a reminder of the night the Quran drove darkness back into the sea.

title: The Rolling Calf
summary: One of Jamaica's most feared duppies, the Rolling Calf appears as a massive jet-black bull with blazing red eyes that gash fire, dragging heavy chains that clank and spark as it moves. It haunts lonely roads, bridle paths through cane fields, and crossroads at night. The Rolling Calf is believed to be the restless spirit of a wicked person — often a cruel butcher or a brutal plantation overseer from slavery days. To escape, one must lie flat in a ditch off the road, scratch a cross in the earth, throw a garment as a decoy, or carry protective herbs like vervain. The legend transforms the chains of slavery into a supernatural symbol of guilt that can be outwitted.
source: FolktalesAmerica.com; Fiwi Roots; Real Jamaica Vacations; Laura Tanna fieldwork
moral: Not all that seems beautiful is safe
full_text:
The night had teeth in Jamaica. Not the gentle darkness of the city, where lampposts push back the dark in pale yellow circles, but the deep country night — the kind that comes when you walk a bridle path through the cane fields and the road is a suggestion rather than a certainty, and the only sound is your own breathing and the occasional cry of a frog somewhere in the marsh.

That was the night Marcus chose to walk home from his grandmother's house in the next village. His grandmother had warned him. 'Boy, the hour is late. Stay until morning.' But Marcus was young and foolish, which is a combination that has caused more trouble in Jamaica than all the duppies in all the graveyards combined.

He was halfway across the Black River plain when he heard it — a sound like iron grinding on stone, slow and terrible, coming from somewhere ahead. Then the chains. Lord Jesus, the chains! They dragged and clanked with a rhythm that did not match any human walk, as though whatever wore them had too many legs or too few, or walked in a way that no creature born of woman should walk.

The cane on either side of the path began to bend away, as though something massive was pushing through. Marcus pressed himself against a tree and held his breath. And then he saw it.

The Rolling Calf.

It was enormous — a bull, but no bull that had ever grazed in any Jamaican pasture. It was jet-black, blacker than the night itself, as if someone had carved a hole in the darkness and given it the shape of rage. Its eyes were red — not the gentle red of a sunset but the angry red of a fire that has found something it intends to burn. Those eyes gashed fire. Actual fire, spitting and crackling, illuminating the path ahead with a hellish glow.

The chains hung from its neck and legs, dragging in the dirt, and where they touched the earth, sparks flew. The smell that preceded it was foul — the smell of grave dirt and old blood and something else, something that made Marcus's stomach turn and his legs go weak as overripe plantain.

Now, Marcus was not a coward. He had killed snakes. He had faced down dogs. But this was no earthly creature.
